---
title: "Particle Mechanics in Special Relativity"
---

## Four-force and four-momentum

To extend Newton's second law to relativistic speeds, we define the *four-force* on a test particle by
$$f^\alpha = m\, \frac{d^2x^\alpha}{d\tau^2}, \tag{1}$$
evaluated at the point $(t_0, \vec x(t_0))$ on its trajectory. Since $m$ and $d\tau$ are invariant, $f^\alpha$ is a contravariant vector. Moreover, given the point and the velocity $\vec v = d\vec x/dt$ there, the boost $\Lambda(-\vec v)$ of [Proposition 3.2](lecture-03.qmd#r-3-2) takes us to coordinates $x'^\alpha$ in which the particle is momentarily at rest:
$$\frac{dx'^i}{dt'} = 0, \qquad d\tau^2 = dt'^2\Bigl(1 - \Bigl|\frac{d\vec x'}{dt'}\Bigr|^2\Bigr) = dt'^2 \quad \text{at } t' = t'_0.$$
In these coordinates (1) reads $f'^0 = 0$ and $f'^i = m\, d^2x'^i/dt'^2 = F^i$, the ordinary Newtonian force. The four-force is thus fixed by the Newtonian force in the rest frame.

::: {.callout-tip .remark-box}

#### **Remark 4.1** (Why proper time?).

Parametrising a worldline $X(\tau)$ by proper time makes the *four-velocity* $U = dX/d\tau = \gamma(1, \vec v)$ transform simply, $U' = \Lambda U$, because $d\tau$ is invariant. Had we used $dX/dt$ instead, both $X$ and $t$ would transform, and the result would not be a vector.
:::

::: {#r-4-2 .callout-note .definition-box}

#### **Definition 4.2** (Four-momentum). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

The *energy-momentum four-vector* of a particle of mass $m$ is
$$p^\alpha = m\, \frac{dx^\alpha}{d\tau}.$$
:::

Using $d\tau = \gamma^{-1} dt$,
$$p^0 = m\gamma = m + \tfrac12 m v^2 + \mathcal O(v^4) = E, \qquad p^i = m\gamma v^i = m v^i + \mathcal O(v^3),$$
the rest energy plus kinetic energy, and the Newtonian momentum. For a photon $d\tau = 0$ and the definition breaks down, but the ratio $v^i = p^i/p^0$ still makes sense.

::: {#r-4-3 .callout-important .proposition-box}

#### **Proposition 4.3** (Mass shell). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

The four-velocity and four-momentum of a massive particle satisfy
$$\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, U^\alpha U^\beta = -1, \qquad \eta_{\alpha\beta}\, p^\alpha p^\beta = -m^2, \qquad E^2 = |\vec p|^2 + m^2.$$

::: {.callout-note .proof-box collapse="true"}

#### Proof

Dividing $d\tau^2 = -\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, dx^\alpha dx^\beta$ by $d\tau^2$ gives $\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, U^\alpha U^\beta = -1$, and multiplying by $m^2$ gives $\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, p^\alpha p^\beta = -m^2$. On the other hand $\eta_{\alpha\beta}\, p^\alpha p^\beta = -(p^0)^2 + |\vec p|^2$, and with $p^0 = E$ the last identity follows. Both contractions are scalars, so they hold in every inertial frame. $\square$
:::
:::

## The energy-momentum tensor

Consider a set of particles labelled by $n$, with $x_n^0(t) = t$. The *density* of four-momentum is
$$T^{\alpha 0}(x) = \sum_n p_n^\alpha(t)\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),$$
with units of momentum per volume, since the delta function has units of inverse volume. The *current* of four-momentum is
$$T^{\alpha i}(x) = \sum_n p_n^\alpha(t)\, \frac{dx_n^i}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),$$
with units of momentum per area per time.

::: {#r-4-4 .callout-note .definition-box}

#### **Definition 4.4** (Energy-momentum tensor of point particles). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

The *energy-momentum tensor* of a system of point particles is
$$T^{\alpha\beta}(x) = \sum_n p_n^\alpha(t)\, \frac{dx_n^\beta}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)). \tag{2}$$
:::

::: {#r-4-5 .callout-important .proposition-box}

#### **Proposition 4.5** (Symmetry and tensor character). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

$T^{\alpha\beta}$ is symmetric and is a Lorentz tensor.

::: {.callout-note .proof-box collapse="true"}

#### Proof

Since $p_n^\alpha = m\, dx_n^\alpha/d\tau$ and $E_n = p_n^0 = m\, dt/d\tau$, we have $dx_n^\beta/dt = p_n^\beta/E_n$, and
$$T^{\alpha\beta}(x) = \sum_n \frac{p_n^\alpha\, p_n^\beta}{E_n}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),$$
which is manifestly symmetric.

For the tensor property, write the three-dimensional delta function as an integral over a four-dimensional one, $\delta^{(4)}(x - x_n(t)) = \delta(x^0 - t)\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t))$, and change variables to proper time:
$$T^{\alpha\beta}(x) = \sum_n \int dt\, p_n^\alpha\, \frac{dx_n^\beta}{dt}\, \delta^{(4)}(x - x_n(t)) = \sum_n \int d\tau\, p_n^\alpha\, \frac{dx_n^\beta}{d\tau}\, \delta^{(4)}(x - x_n(\tau)).$$
The four-dimensional delta function is a Lorentz scalar: $\int d^4x\, \delta^{(4)}(x) = 1$ and $d^4x$ is invariant because $\det\Lambda = 1$. So $T^{\alpha\beta}$ is a product of two contravariant vectors integrated against a scalar. Note that this argument fails for the three-dimensional delta function, and for general coordinate transformations, whose Jacobian need not be one. $\square$
:::
:::

The symmetry of $T^{\alpha\beta}$ says that the flux of the $\alpha$-component of momentum across a surface of constant $x^\beta$ equals the flux of the $\beta$-component across a surface of constant $x^\alpha$. It is what makes angular momentum conserved, as we see below.

::: {#r-4-6 .callout-important .proposition-box}

#### **Proposition 4.6** (Conservation of energy and momentum). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

If the particles are free, or interact only in collisions localised at points (in which four-momentum is conserved), then
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\beta}\, T^{\alpha\beta} = 0. \tag{3}$$
If the particles are acted on by four-forces $f_n^\alpha$, then instead $\partial_\beta T^{\alpha\beta} = G^\alpha$ with
$$G^\alpha(x) = \sum_n \frac{d\tau_n}{dt}\, f_n^\alpha\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)).$$

::: {.callout-note .proof-box collapse="true"}

#### Proof

Since $\partial_{x^i}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n) = -\partial_{x_n^i}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n)$,
$$\begin{aligned}
\partial_i T^{\alpha i} &= -\sum_n p_n^\alpha\, \frac{dx_n^i}{dt}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x_n^i}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)) = -\sum_n p_n^\alpha\, \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)) \\
&= -\partial_0 T^{\alpha 0} + \sum_n \frac{dp_n^\alpha}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)).
\end{aligned}$$
For free particles $dp_n^\alpha/dt = 0$; with localised collisions the sum of the changes vanishes at each collision point. Otherwise $dp_n^\alpha/dt = (d\tau_n/dt) f_n^\alpha$, which gives $G^\alpha$. $\square$
:::
:::

The energy-momentum tensor is the conserved Noether current of spacetime translations $x^\alpha \mapsto x^\alpha + a^\alpha$ (see [Invariance and conservation](../noethers-wonderful-theorem/lecture-01.html#invariance-and-conservation) in my notes on Noether's theorem): its time components express conservation of energy and its space components conservation of momentum.

::: {#r-4-7 .callout-important .proposition-box}

#### **Proposition 4.7** (Total four-momentum). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

If $T^{\alpha\beta}$ vanishes at spatial infinity, the total four-momentum
$$p^\alpha_{\text{tot}} = \int d^3x\, T^{\alpha 0}(x)$$
is conserved.

::: {.callout-note .proof-box collapse="true"}

#### Proof

By (3) and the divergence theorem,
$$\frac{dp^\alpha_{\text{tot}}}{dt} = \int d^3x\, \partial_0 T^{\alpha 0} = -\int d^3x\, \partial_i T^{\alpha i} = 0. \qquad \square$$
:::
:::

## Angular momentum and spin

::: {#r-4-8 .callout-note .definition-box}

#### **Definition 4.8** (Angular momentum). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

The *angular momentum density* and the *total angular momentum* are
$$M^{\gamma\alpha\beta} = x^\alpha T^{\beta\gamma} - x^\beta T^{\alpha\gamma}, \qquad J^{\alpha\beta} = \int d^3x\, M^{0\alpha\beta}.$$
:::

Using (3), $\partial_\gamma M^{\gamma\alpha\beta} = T^{\beta\alpha} - T^{\alpha\beta} = 0$ by [Proposition 4.5](#r-4-5). Since $M^{\gamma\alpha\beta}$ is antisymmetric in $\alpha\beta$, these are six continuity equations, and $J^{\alpha\beta}$ is conserved.

Of these six, the components $J^{0i} = t\, p^i_{\text{tot}} - \int d^3x\, x^i T^{00}$ carry no new information: choosing the origin so that $\int d^3x\, x^i T^{00} = 0$ at $t = 0$ makes $J^{0i}$ vanish then, and hence at all times, since $p^i_{\text{tot}}$ is conserved. The physical components are
$$J^{ij} = \int d^3x\, \bigl(x^i T^{j0} - x^j T^{i0}\bigr),$$
which have the structure of $L_i = \epsilon_{ijk}\, x_j p_k$: we identify $(J^{23}, J^{31}, J^{12})$ with the three components of angular momentum. $J$ contains both an orbital and an intrinsic part.

Under a translation $x^\alpha \mapsto x^\alpha + a^\alpha$,
$$J^{\alpha\beta} \mapsto J^{\alpha\beta} + a^\alpha p^\beta_{\text{tot}} - a^\beta p^\alpha_{\text{tot}}, \tag{4}$$
since orbital angular momentum is defined with respect to a centre of rotation. The intrinsic part should not depend on that choice.

::: {#r-4-9 .callout-note .definition-box}

#### **Definition 4.9** (Spin). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

The *spin* four-vector is
$$S_\alpha = \tfrac12\, \epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\, J^{\beta\gamma}\, U^\delta, \qquad U^\delta = \frac{p^\delta_{\text{tot}}}{\sqrt{-\eta_{\mu\nu}\, p^\mu_{\text{tot}}\, p^\nu_{\text{tot}}}},$$
where $U^\delta$ is the four-velocity of the centre of mass.
:::

::: {#r-4-10 .callout-important .proposition-box}

#### **Proposition 4.10** (Properties of spin). [[1, Ch. 2]](#ref-1)

$S_\alpha$ is invariant under translations and satisfies $S_\alpha U^\alpha = 0$. In the centre-of-mass frame, $U = (1, 0, 0, 0)$, it is $S = (0, J^{23}, J^{31}, J^{12})$.

::: {.callout-note .proof-box collapse="true"}

#### Proof

By (4), a translation adds to $S_\alpha$ terms proportional to $\epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\, a^\beta U^\gamma U^\delta$ (since $p_{\text{tot}} \propto U$), which vanish because $\epsilon$ is antisymmetric and $U^\gamma U^\delta$ symmetric in $\gamma\delta$. The same argument gives $S_\alpha U^\alpha \propto \epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\, J^{\beta\gamma} U^\delta U^\alpha = 0$. In the centre-of-mass frame only $\delta = 0$ contributes, and the components can be read off. $\square$
:::
:::

## Charges and currents

The same construction applies to electric charge. The *charge density*, the *current density* and the *four-current* of a set of particles with charges $e_n$ are
$$\varepsilon(x) = \sum_n e_n\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)), \qquad \vec j(x) = \sum_n e_n\, \frac{d\vec x_n}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)),$$
$$J^\alpha(x) = \sum_n e_n\, \frac{dx_n^\alpha}{dt}\, \delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x_n(t)), \qquad x_n^0 = t,$$
so that $J^\alpha = (\varepsilon, \vec j)$. Charge is never created or destroyed, and the argument of [Proposition 4.6](#r-4-6), with $p_n^\alpha$ replaced by the constants $e_n$, gives
$$\partial_\alpha J^\alpha = 0.$$
Hence the total charge $Q = \int d^3x\, J^0$ is constant in time. The electromagnetic field itself is the subject of the next lecture.
